ownership_reason:
readOldBinaryEntry reads the header of the old binary format. It returns without consuming the NUL byte that pads the 26-byte header plus the NUL-terminated name to an even length. Data reading therefore starts one byte early, and the first data byte returned is that pad byte (0).

The writer side is pinned as correct. CpioArchiveOutputStream.writeOldBinaryEntry pads header plus name to a multiple of two. Before reading anything, the trigger asserts the archive length that exactly this layout produces: 86 = 26+9+1 (header) + 11+1 (data) + 26+11+1 (trailer). That assertion passes on the variant; without the header pads the length would be 84.

Both sides apply the same 2-byte alignment to binary data: CpioArchiveInputStream.read and CpioArchiveOutputStream.closeArchiveEntry both pad data to 2 for FORMAT_OLD_BINARY. The new-format header reader readNewEntry ends with pad(getHeaderSize() + namesize, 4), mirroring writeNewEntry. So each format-specific header reader consumes its own header pad.

The shared helpers readCString and read serve formats with different alignment rules (old ASCII has none). Two passing tests show they are correct: CpioArchiveInputStreamTest.testNewFormatRoundTrip sends the same odd-length name through readCString and read in the new format, and testCpioUnarchive reads bla.cpio, whose new-format headers are padded. The minimal repair restores pad(ret.getHeaderSize() + namesize, 2) as the last step of readOldBinaryEntry.
trigger: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.CpioTestCase::testBinaryFormatRoundTrip. It writes one entry ("data.txt", 11 bytes "binary cpio", mode C_ISREG|0644, time 1000) with CpioArchiveOutputStream in FORMAT_OLD_BINARY, asserts the archive length is 86, then reads it back with CpioArchiveInputStream. It asserts the name and size, copies the data with IOUtils.copy, and compares byte by byte with the message "byte i".
